references.text: God commands Noah to bring two of every living creature into the ark, a male and a female, to keep them alive during the flood.
Noah receives instructions to take seven pairs of each clean animal species and one pair of the unclean animals, as well as seven pairs of birds, to preserve their kinds on earth.
The clean and unclean animals, birds, and creeping things came to Noah in pairs and entered the ark, just as God had commanded—a close parallel to verse 15.
God breathed the breath of life into humanity, and the expression 'ruach chayyim' (breath of life) in 7:15 connects to this fundamental description of life-giving breath.
Everything that had the breath of life (nishmat ruach chayyim) in its nostrils died—a contrast to the animals saved in the ark because they possessed the breath of life (ruach chayyim).
Noah's faith and obedience led him to build the ark and save his household, a testimony to the power of faith linked to the flood narrative.
Verse 9 confirms that the animals' entry occurred under God's explicit command, emphasizing the divine order behind the flood.
Verse 7 complements verse 15 by showing that salvation in the ark included both humans (Noah's household) and animals, with both groups entering at the same time.
Matthew uses the timing of Noah's entry (described in 7:15) as a decisive turning point to illustrate sudden judgment upon a worldly world.
Luke confirms Matthew's interpretation by using Noah's entry as a clear picture of the final judgment that strikes a worldly world.
1 Peter specifies the number saved ('eight souls') and interprets the floodwaters as a symbol of baptism, giving the historical event a new theological dimension.
